name: Shark liver oil

lead: Shark liver oil is extracted from the livers of deep-sea sharks. It contains squalene, a lipid that also occurs in human skin oil, and alkylglycerols. Skin-care makers have used squalene from the oil as an emollient, and it is sold as a capsule supplement that proponents associate with immune support, joint comfort and recovery, which they connect to training and general wellbeing.

Human research includes small trials on blood lipids, plasmalogens, inflammation markers and red-cell fatty acids, and a long line of reviews on alkylglycerols. Research on its direct effect on appearance is limited to the broader literature on squalene in cosmetic dermatology.

paras: Most people take it as capsules or liquid oil, sometimes alongside fish oil. In cosmetics, squalene (often now plant-derived or hydrogenated to squalane) is blended into creams and lotions as a moisturiser. In forums, it appears in supplement stacks for joints and recovery.

Reported side effects include nausea, stomach upset and diarrhoea, and people with seafood allergy may react. Studies have found PCB and PBDE contamination in some supplements. The deep-sea shark species harvested for liver oil are assessed as endangered or critically endangered by the IUCN, and the oil's origin is an environmental controversy.

chain: Skin moisture; claimed immune, joint and recovery support
angle.text: Squalene from shark liver oil has been used in moisturisers to soften skin, and the oil is also taken orally by people who connect its claimed immune and joint effects to recovery and a better physique. The route to appearance is via skin care or via supporting training.

lead: Shark liver oil (SLO) is the lipid fraction of the livers of sharks, especially deep-sea species such as gulper and school sharks. It is rich in squalene (up to about 90 percent of the oil in some species) and in alkylglycerols, ether-linked lipids [1][2][3]. It is sold as a dietary supplement and has long supplied squalene to skin-care products.

For appearance, the link is through skin and recovery. Squalene is a main component of human sebum and has been studied for emollient and antioxidant properties in cosmetic dermatology [4]; shark liver oil was historically the richest source. Supplement users also take the oil for joint comfort and general health, which they tie to training capacity and recovery.

Folk medicine in Scandinavia used the oil for wound healing and respiratory and digestive complaints, and production rose in World War II as a vitamin A source [5][1]. Research includes randomised trials of metabolic and lipid effects and reviews of alkylglycerols; environmental concerns over shark harvesting are well documented [6][1].

Source species IUCN-listed endangered or critically endangered [1]

paras: Sharks lack a swim bladder and use large, oil-filled livers for buoyancy; squalene can make up most of the oil in some deep-sea species [1]. Alkylglycerols, studied since the mid-twentieth century, are ether lipids that have been investigated for effects on blood formation, immune function and tumour growth [7][8][3]. Pristane is a minor component [1].

Squalene is a key intermediate in cholesterol biosynthesis and is found in human sebum at roughly 13 percent of the surface lipids, which is why cosmetic chemists use it and its hydrogenated form squalane in moisturisers [4][9].

sections.h: Uses in skin care and supplements
paras: Squalene derived from shark liver oil has been a skin-care ingredient, valued for emollient, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and the oil itself is a component of some moisturising lotions [4][1]. Because of overexploitation, alternative sources (plant oils and microbial production) are being developed [6].

As a supplement, shark liver oil is taken for immunity, inflammation and joint support. T Nation forum posts show users taking it for joints or on a nutritionist's advice while describing the taste as strong [10][11].

A randomised controlled trial in people with features of metabolic disease reported that shark liver oil supplementation enriched plasmalogens and reduced markers of dyslipidaemia and inflammation [12]. A six-week trial in young healthy women found short-term supplementation changed the fatty-acid composition of erythrocyte membranes [13]. A randomised trial of alkylglycerols in obese individuals reported lower serum complement and plasma VEGF [14]. Earlier clinical reports concerned alkoxyglycerol in cancer treatment [15].
Reviews of squalene's biological actions describe antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in vivo and in vitro [16]. No trial of oral shark liver oil on skin appearance or hair was found.

Reported side effects include nausea, upset stomach and diarrhoea; seafood-allergic people may react, and safe dose ranges have not been established [1]. A 2006 Japanese study found PCB and PBDE contamination in some supplements [1]. Animal studies suggested the oil might raise blood cholesterol [1].

The deep-sea shark species used are slow-reproducing and the IUCN lists school, gulper and basking sharks as endangered or critically endangered; harvesting for squalene is a conservation concern [1][6].
